name: Baby oil tanning
lead: Baby oil tanning is the practice of applying baby oil or similar oils to the skin before sun exposure, in the belief that it speeds or deepens a tan. Because such oils typically contain no sunscreen filter, the practice is associated with greater sunburn risk [1].

Oils were a long-standing tanning aid: Jean Patou launched what is described as the first sun tan oil, Huile de Chaldee, in 1927, and baby oil was commonly used to increase tanning in the 1950s [1]. Sunscreens with SPF ratings began appearing from 1962 onward, and a shift toward protective products followed [1].

paras: Practitioners apply a plain oil to skin before sunbathing. Proponents have historically said the oil helps skin look bronzed and tan faster. Tanning oils and later lotions, including intensifiers and accelerators, formed part of the commercial tanning industry [1].

UVB causes DNA damage in skin cells, which triggers new melanin production, producing a tan that appears two or three days later; UVA oxidizes existing melanin for a faster darkening that does not add protection [1]. Public health bodies classify UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen [2].
No studies found. Research on UV exposure and tanning in general links sunburn and tanning-device use to higher melanoma risk [1][2].

Sunburn is the most common risk of UV exposure, and overexposure is linked to skin cancer, photoageing and immune effects [1]. Sunscreen reduces sunburn but also slows tanning, which is why tan-seekers have sometimes avoided it [1].

timeline.event: Jean Patou launches Huile de Chaldee, described as the first sun tan oil. [1]
Baby oil commonly used to increase tanning. [1]

card.summary: Oiling up to tan faster, a mid-century habit that adds no UV protection and has no studies behind its claimed benefit.
card.note: Plain oils contain no sunscreen filter; UV exposure is linked to sunburn and skin cancer.

quick.overview:
Baby oil tanning means rubbing baby oil or a tanning oil on the skin before sunbathing, with the aim of tanning faster. It was common in the 1950s and persists as a folk practice.

No studies were found testing whether plain oil improves tanning.
quick.mechanism: People do this in the belief that oil helps skin absorb or intensify sun. UV light itself drives tanning by triggering melanin production, and the oil does not change that process in any documented way.
quick.risks: Oils without a sunscreen filter provide no UV protection. Sunburn and UV-linked skin cancer are documented risks of sun exposure generally.
